title: Scientists Made a Computer Memory Out of DNA — It Uses 100x Less Power!
summary:
Did you know that one tiny gram of DNA can store 215 million gigabytes of data? That's like fitting millions of movies on a single speck! Scientists have wanted to use DNA in electronics for a long time, but it was hard to make it work with regular computer parts. Now, researchers at Penn State have figured out a way.

They created a new kind of memory device called a memristor. A memristor is special because it can remember information even after the power is turned off — kind of like your brain remembers things. The team used two main ingredients: synthetic DNA and a material called perovskite (which is also used in solar cells).

Here's the cool part: they added tiny silver particles to the DNA. This made the DNA able to conduct electricity, like a wire. The DNA also helped organize the perovskite into neat layers. When they put it all together, the device worked using less than 0.1 volt of electricity. To compare, a wall outlet in your house has 120 volts! That means it uses 100 times less power than a regular flash drive.

The device also stayed working in very hot temperatures — up to 250 degrees Fahrenheit — and kept working for more than six weeks at room temperature. That's much better than other perovskite memory devices.

Why does this matter? As artificial intelligence (AI) gets bigger, computers need to store more information without using too much energy. This DNA-based memory could help make future computers faster and more efficient. The scientists even think it could lead to computers that work more like the human brain. So next time you see DNA in a science class, remember: it might be the future of computer memory!
why_it_matters: Using less power in computers could help the environment and make future devices, games, and AI smarter without draining so much energy.

background_read: DNA is the molecule inside living things that stores life's instructions; its ability to pack huge amounts of data into a tiny space makes it interesting for computer storage.
Penn State is a large university in Pennsylvania where scientists study materials, including the perovskite used here.
Perovskite is a mineral-like material already used in some solar cells, and scientists keep testing new uses for it.
Article_Structure: WHO: Researchers at Penn State created the DNA-based memory device.
WHAT: They built a memristor using synthetic DNA, perovskite, and tiny silver particles that conduct electricity.
WHERE: In the lab, the device worked on less than 0.1 volt, survived high heat, and lasted more than six weeks at room temperature.
WHY: Scientists want low-power computer memory as artificial intelligence grows, and future computers may need to work more like the human brain.

perspectives.description: They see DNA memory as a step toward faster, brain-like computers that use only a tiny amount of electricity.
They would want to see the device work reliably in everyday conditions and connect with existing computer parts before it replaces flash drives.
They worry about the growing power demands of AI data centers, so a low-power memory device could help reduce that strain.
